## Chapter 2

Hay's diplomatic triumph in China lifted Adams's spirits, but King's collapse and Hay's failing health darkened the season; meanwhile the magnet on Adams's desk, and the geologists' confessions of ignorance, warned him that the unity he had sought all his life was dissolving into a multiplicity science could no longer pretend to govern.

Inevitable Paris beckoned. No other city still taught on every side—theatres, salons, beaux-arts, Gothic stones, theology and its antitheses—yet the effect was chaos, more complex even than New York’s, and he could do no more than keep a little in front of the movement, lest it run him down.

One duty so long postponed that it had become a reproach—Baireuth—was despatched at last. There, the master’s spirit no longer brooded as in 1876. The rococo frame jarred. Wagner was now as familiar as Shakespeare; the frenzies of New York and the coquetries of Paris, which had turned his music into a language of catastrophe, were more Wagnerian than Baireuth itself. The “Götterdämmerung” that once terrified had become a musical philology. He listened, learned what the master supposed himself to mean, and passed on.

For theory he had his private jest of “conservative Christian anarchy”—a phrase only to mark the paradox that, in the last synthesis, order and anarchy were one, and the unity was chaos. If the end was inevitability, then duty was acceleration: to multiply force, reduce friction, heighten velocity, push the present to its break. The jest served him only so far as a student’s talisman can serve: a name for the law that was hurrying him out of the nineteenth century.

The true school, that year, lay eastward. Russia drew him on, and from the first glimpse—at some wayside Polish station, a Jew crouched in misery on the platform; at the last, a peasant kneeling in the St. Petersburg station to kiss an ikon—every sign read the same: conservative, Christian, anarchic; an energy of pure inertia. To study it in the dry light of his paradox made it luminous like the salt of radium, but with negative glow, as though the substance had been sucked of its active force. It seemed a camp of tribes that had wandered to a halt and lost the habit of motion without learning the art of permanence; a country that acted as a sink of energy, keeping the uniformity of ice and snow.

Could such inertia of race be broken? The question was old even in America. He put it, cautiously, to those whose business it was to answer—men like the finance minister and the minister of ways—who had driven the huge machine at vast expense for a dozen years. Their frankness helped little. The stimulus had been violent; the peasant remained the peasant; since 1898 the pace lagged. A tourist-student who knew that, in his own country, the best secretaries and presidents could not foresee a single generation, grew docile to ignorance. Let one allow a generation, or two: the acceleration might still leave the gap unchanged.

Germany attracted his companions; he, who had had enough of Berlin forty years before, fled north. Sweden, with its southern light after St. Petersburg’s stern streets, lured him; and thence he crept to the world’s edge. In the equinoctial twilight at Hammerfest, electric lamps burned a steady day against the polar night, and, more wonderful still, the cable brought, hour by hour, the bulletins of McKinley’s wound and death, with Hay’s and Roosevelt’s words, hot from Washington—a miracle of unity that seemed to correct the very faults of the solar system. The electro-dynamo-social universe worked better than the sun.

The acceleration was marvellous—and wholly in lines of unity—yet the same fjords, watched from the same snow-patches by the same Lapps and reindeer, pressed back with the old ice-cap of negation. One day’s steaming north would bring him against the barrier; he had never before met a ne plus ultra. From that ridge of rock he looked south over the old division-line—Baltic to Black Sea—that had stood since ice and inertia first took charge, indifferent to climate or soil. Russia and the ice pressed; his fisherman ancestors had stared at the same obstacles; their problem was his.

He floated back by the western rim: Kiel, Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne. Here was a Germany new to mankind. Hamburg was almost American; Düsseldorf, black with coal-soot; Cologne a railway centre that wore its finished cathedral like a Chicago heirloom. In 1858 the old north-German plain was still the prehistoric highway between Asia and the ocean; Russia was felt at Cologne more strongly than France. In 1901 Russia had disappeared from the lines of force. Coal alone persisted—from the Ruhr to Picardy—and stamped the land with the same mark one saw at Birmingham or Pittsburgh. The river produced the power; the power produced the people; the people produced the mind; the mind obeyed the motor.

From Hammerfest to Cherbourg on one shore; from Halifax to Norfolk on the other—one empire owned one emperor—Coal. Jealousies might divide it, but the unity was real. Beyond it, Russia—older, perhaps surer, because it rested on the eternal law of inertia—held its own. The personal stake in this balance grew practical. That mass of inertia was moving, irresistibly, over China; and Hay stood athwart its path. So long as the finance minister ruled, Hay was safe; should he fall, Hay would totter.

Measured as education, the triangles closed. Paris had shown the chaos of creation; Baireuth, the jaded frame that could no longer hold its god; Russia, the luminosity of negation; Hammerfest, the miracle of unified force; the Rhine, the empire of coal. The student, who had set out to keep in front of the movement, found himself again between unity and multiplicity, God and the magnet, Hay’s combine and the peasant’s ikon, and no nearer to a decision than before—except that acceleration was irresistible and that the line of division, like the ice, never forgot.

## Chapter 3

America takes tragedy lightly; the machine refuses to pause. Yet 1901 made of Hay a figure walking from funeral to funeral: first his son; then, with hideous suddenness at the last, his chief; and in a California inn, alone and uncared-for, Clarence King, “the best and brightest man of his generation,” went out. Ça vous amuse, la vie?

Adams landed to go at once to King’s funeral, and thence to a Washington which had suffered a revolution. A generation he had thought of as boys suddenly stood in front; the men of his age were old, at once. Whatever might be said for office as a school, his course there was finished.

As for Roosevelt, they could not take him in his old character, and could not recover him in the new. Power, wielded by abnormal energy, is the most serious of facts, and Roosevelt, more than any man within range of notoriety, was pure act. With him in the White House, wielding unmeasured force with immeasurable energy, the relation of elder to younger—teacher to pupil—ceased to be possible. Even Hay’s place was false; Adams’s ended of itself. A friend in power was a friend lost.

History keeps few truths worth hoarding, but human nature holds its proverbs. Lucius Seneca could have told one all that needed saying; he learned, at last, that a pupil named Nero was an ultimate lesson. In a milder key one might insist on the aphorism: power is poison. Presidents showed it always—first in violent stimulation, then in worse reaction—and even the best-balanced mind cannot seize unlimited force without being maddened by the packs that snarl for it and live by it. Roosevelt’s nature was direct and honest, yet his first year’s chronic excitement made a friend tremble. The effect of unlimited power on a limited mind is worth noting in Presidents because it marks the same process in society. Somewhere, self-control must fail before the control of the infinite.

Hay, meanwhile, declined only in strength; Lodge, by law of position. He stood at once as the President’s friend and as an independent statesman; either posture demanded more balance than Massachusetts—various, exacting, multiplying standards—would long allow. The old Boston malady—Bostonitis—had grown acute. Banks, clergy, Harvard, immigrants, socialists—each stamped a rival die. New power disintegrated society; money spent itself to hold the machine together. No single man could represent it.

As a type for study Lodge was the more instructive. Roosevelts are born; Lodges are made. English to his last fibre in taste and tradition; revolted by most Continental virtues; happy among Shakespeare’s excesses; an excellent talker, voracious reader, ready wit, clear mind, powerful memory; yet shifting his weight from one sensitive muscle to another—Yankee, pure American, Irish patriot, Harvard scholar—he betrayed the race-consciousness that is Boston’s grace and torment. Double standards—delight of letters, snare of politicians—threatened him; the shifty sands of opinion had a trick of giving way.

In such games an elderly friend found no profit but the amusement of the acrobat. Domestic politics had sunk into a contest of machines and men who served them; the larger study vanished in the ambitions of fifth-rate actors. There was one field, still, where a mere scholar could see his work: foreign affairs. The work of domestic progress is done by masses of mechanical power—steam, electric, furnace—which have to be controlled by a score of men. Most of them have nothing to tell; they are forces as dumb as their dynamos, trustees for the public because they hold the switches. Whoever manages the property, the power will remain what it is, and will control society without appeal, as it controls its stokers and pit-men. Modern politics is, at bottom, a struggle not of men but of forces. The men become every year more and more creatures of force, massed about central power-houses. The conflict is no longer between the men, but between the motors that drive the men, and the men tend to succumb to their own motive forces.

For history, then, international relation is the only sure base for a map. The Secretary of State, obliged to look round and far ahead, measures forces unknown to party managers, and finds Congress hostile as Congress has been since Congress began. He exists to recognize a world the Senate prefers to ignore; to own obligations it repudiates when it can; to sign bargains it strives to turn to account or to reject. The Senate has intrigued against him from the first day of its life, and intrigues still.

This suited the scholar’s need. Hay required no counsel; he wrote no state papers to be helped; he had a nation behind him such as history had never conceived; but to a docile pupil he could teach the only lesson worth learning—to triangulate the future and fix, if one could, the acceleration of movement in politics, as one tried to fix it in philosophy and physics, in finance and force. “Theory and practice” were twin feet; a man must march on both or go astray. If education could be brought to its height, it was here, for never had two minds—Hay’s and his chief’s—been more completely trained by events, nor the world’s machinery made freer to supply the last and best information. Yet the result, to the pupil, was grotesque. Never had his ignorance looked so appalling. He seemed to know nothing—to be falling in space—and the worst depth was the incredibility that no one knew more. Even could the Czar, the Kaiser, and the Mikado turn schoolmasters and tell their inmost thought, the lesson would end in the same confession. Only by comparing ignorances could he measure his own.

Hay's last triumphs—drawing England, France, and even Germany toward an Atlantic combine while Russia alone remained intractable—seemed to Adams the highest reach a scholar of statesmanship could witness, even as he confessed that such mastery only deepened his sense of his own ignorance.
